routine.name: Combine
routine.what: Two or three short sentences, one idea. Put them together without losing anything.
routine.why: A reader who can only write short sentences reads long ones as a list of facts. Combining is the same skill from the other side.

routine.name: Expand
routine.what: One plain sentence. Add when, where, how or why — not another sentence.
routine.why: The kernel is already true. What gets added is where the meaning lives, and this is the move that shows that.

routine.name: Because · but · so
routine.what: One stem, finished three ways. Each conjunction forces a different kind of thinking.
routine.why: Two minutes, and it reveals whether a child understood the text at all. Because asks for a cause, but asks for a tension, so asks for a result.

from: The Declaration of Independence is short.
Most of it is legal, not poetic.
It lists complaints.
It states a principle.
It announces a decision.
to: The Declaration of Independence is a short document, and most of what it does is legal rather than poetic.
It lists grievances, states a principle, and announces a decision.
The famous sentence is in the second paragraph.

from: Unalienable is a legal term.
An unalienable right cannot be given away.
Not even the owner can surrender it.
That is a stronger claim than a protected right.
to: Unalienable is a legal term, not a flourish.
A right that is unalienable cannot be transferred or surrendered, even by the person who holds it, which makes it a different and stronger claim than a right that is merely protected.

from: Length is the first reason.
Probe is four letters.
Investigation is thirteen.
Bid replaces attempt.
Eye replaces is considering.
That saves a line of type.
to: Length is the first reason.
Probe is four letters and investigation is thirteen.
Bid replaces attempt, slam replaces criticise sharply, and eye replaces is considering, which saves a line of type.

from: A headline must fit a column.
So newspapers use short words.
Officials do not vow in conversation.
A disagreement becomes a rift only in print.
to: A headline has to fit a column, so newspapers developed a vocabulary of short words that rarely appear anywhere else.
Officials do not vow in conversation, and a disagreement only becomes a rift in print.

from: The time limit is awkward too.
Horses were native to North America.
They died out there.
Europeans brought them back.
So a wild horse may count either way.
to: The time limit is just as awkward.
Horses were native to North America, went extinct there, and returned with Europeans, so whether a wild horse is a returning native or an introduction depends on where a person puts the line.

from: Invasive is a technical word with a military word inside it.
The metaphor does real work.
It suggests an attacker with a plan.
A plant does not move that way.
to: Invasive is a technical term with a military word inside it, and the metaphor does real work.
It suggests an attacker arriving with intent, which is not how a plant or a fish moves anywhere.

items.title: The Shape of a Science Article

from: A research paper looks like prose.
It works like a form.
Every one has the same five parts.
They come in the same order.
to: A research paper looks like prose and works like a form.
Every one has the same five parts in the same order, and a scientist reading it does not start at the beginning.

from: The abstract comes first.
It is written last.
It is a short version of the whole paper.
Most readers stop there.
to: The abstract comes first and is written last.
It is a compressed version of the whole paper, and most readers decide from it alone whether to read any further.

from: You can find it by its words.
However.
Admittedly.
Critics argue.
Each one warns you that the next sentence will not agree with the last.
to: You can find it by its words.
However, admittedly, it is true that, critics argue — each one announces that the next sentence will not continue the paragraph before it.

from: Most good arguments change direction once.
The writer builds a case.
Then the writer takes the other side seriously.
Then the writer answers it.
That stop is the turn.
to: Most arguments worth reading change direction once.
The writer builds a case, then stops and takes the other side seriously, then answers it.
That stop is the turn, and it usually arrives in the middle.

from: Open a history chapter.
The first thing is often a timeline.
It is easy to skip.
Skipping it makes the chapter harder later.
to: Open a history chapter and the first thing on the page is usually a timeline.
It is easy to skip, and skipping it is why the chapter gets harder three pages later.

from: A timeline does one job the prose cannot.
It fixes the order in one glance.
Then the reader is not holding dates in mind.
to: A timeline does one job the prose cannot.
It fixes the order of events in a single glance, so the reader is not holding dates in mind while also following an argument.

from: The best sentence often admits what went wrong.
A thermometer read in a warm room.
A timer started late.
That is not a confession.
It explains the number.
to: The sentence that makes a conclusion work is usually the one admitting what went wrong.
A thermometer read in a warm room, a timer started late — naming it is not a confession, it is the reason the number came out as it did.

from: Students are told a lab report ends with a conclusion.
They are also told to write a summary.
Those two instructions pull apart.
to: Students are often taught that a lab report ends with a conclusion, and then taught to write the conclusion as a summary.
Those two instructions pull in opposite directions.

expand.kernel: The question at the front and the answer at the back hold the report together.
expand.expanded: The question at the front and the answer at the back hold the report together, and everything between them is there to get from one to the other.

expand.kernel: A conclusion that says what to do next is stronger.
expand.expanded: A conclusion that ends with what to do next is stronger than one that ends with a result.

from: The main story has to move.
A sidebar holds what would break that movement.
A definition.
A short history.
The numbers behind a claim.
to: The main story has to move.
A sidebar holds the material that would break that movement: a definition, a short history, the numbers behind a claim, a second voice that does not fit the narrative.

from: A sidebar can hold the part the writer is least sure of.
A disputed figure.
A claim from one source.
The box marks it as separate without hiding it.
to: A sidebar can also carry the part the writer is least sure of.
A disputed figure, a claim from one source only — putting it in a box marks it as separate from the reporting without hiding it.

from: A park brochure and a resort brochure can describe the same valley.
Both can be accurate.
They leave opposite impressions.
Neither has to lie to do it.
to: A national park brochure and a resort brochure for the same valley can both be accurate and leave opposite impressions.
Neither has to lie to do it, and neither usually does.

from: The resort brochure shows the same trail in good light.
It does not mention the storms.
Everything in it is true.
The storms are missing.
to: The resort brochure photographs the same trail in good light and does not mention the storms.
Everything in it is true, and the storms are missing, and that absence is the point.

expand.kernel: Every choice in it follows from that.
expand.expanded: It is what each one needs you to do after reading it — stay safe, or book a room — and every choice in it follows from that.

items.title: The Scientist and the Press Release

from: A study is published.
A university writes a press release.
A news site writes a story from the release.
By the end the claim is often larger.
to: A study is published, a university writes a press release about it, and a news site writes a story from the release.
By the end of that chain the claim is often larger than the study.

from: The study is careful.
It says an association was seen in a sample of one size.
It says the conditions were particular.
It says more work is needed.
to: The study is written to be careful.
It says that an association was observed in a sample of a particular size, under particular conditions, and that further work is needed.

expand.kernel: Studies of this chain found most of the exaggeration is already in the release.
expand.expanded: Studies of this chain have found that most of the exaggeration in health reporting is already present in the release, not added by the journalist.

items.title: A Letter to the Editor About the Dam

from: The argument is about memory.
The writer swam in that reservoir as a child.
The letter names three families who did the same.
It asks what the town will be without it.
to: The argument is about memory.
The writer swam in that reservoir as a child, names three families who did the same, and asks what the town will be without it.

from: A letter in a small-town paper says the old dam should stay.
It runs four hundred words.
It never says what the writer does for a living.
It is signed with a name and a street.
to: A letter in a small-town paper argues that the old dam should stay.
It runs four hundred words and never says what the writer does for a living.
It is signed with a name and a street.

items.title: Why the Museum Label Says Probably

from: Date ranges work the same way.
1480 to 1520 is not vagueness.
It is the span the evidence allows.
Narrowing it would claim too much.
to: Date ranges work the same way.
1480 to 1520 is not vagueness; it is the span the evidence allows, and narrowing it would be claiming more than the museum can support.

from: A museum label is about forty words long.
Every word has been argued over.
The hedges are not caution for its own sake.
They record how much is known.
to: A museum label is about forty words long and every one of them has been argued over.
The hedges in it are not caution for its own sake.
They are a record of how much is actually known.

expand.kernel: A label with no qualifiers is either very well evidenced or written by somebody who has stopped checking.
expand.expanded: A label with no qualifiers anywhere is either very well evidenced or written by somebody who has stopped distinguishing what is known from what is assumed.

items.title: The Company's Report on the River

from: A plant is accused of polluting a river.
Three reports usually appear.
The company writes one.
The state agency writes one.
A university lab writes one.
All three may use the same samples.
to: When a plant is accused of polluting a river, three reports usually appear.
The company writes one, the state agency writes one, and a university lab writes one, and all three may use the same samples.

from: The company's report does not have to lie.
It selects.
It reports readings downstream after the spring melt.
The river is highest then.
Anything in it is most dilute.
to: The company's report is not required to lie and generally does not.
It selects.
It reports the readings downstream of the outfall after the spring melt, when the river is highest and anything in it is most dilute.

expand.kernel: Where they sampled, when, and what they compared it to explains most of the disagreement.
expand.expanded: Where they sampled, when, and what they compared it to will explain most of the disagreement before you reach anybody's opinion.

expand.kernel: All three print who funded them, usually near the back.
expand.expanded: Who funded each one is printed somewhere in all three, usually near the back.

from: The graph does the rest.
It shows mass balance each year since 1950.
The ice loses more each summer than it gains each winter.
The slope steepens after 1990.
to: The graph beside them does the rest.
A line of annual mass balance, measured every year since 1950, shows the ice losing more each summer than it gains each winter, and the slope steepening after 1990.

from: The table holds the numbers.
It gives mean loss per decade.
It gives the uncertainty beside each figure.
It is the only part you can check the line against.
to: The table underneath is where the numbers live.
Mean loss per decade, in meters of water equivalent, with the uncertainty beside each figure — unglamorous, and the only part that lets you check the line.

expand.kernel: A glacier photograph from 1920 beside one from today is persuasive.
expand.expanded: A photograph of a glacier taken in 1920 beside one from today is the most persuasive thing in any article about ice.

items.title: A Map, a Table, and a Flood

from: The map shades the flooded area.
It is the only one that shows where.
It treats every shaded house the same.
Water at the doorstep looks like water at the ceiling.
to: The map shades the flooded area.
It is the only one that shows where, and it treats every shaded house the same, whether the water came to the doorstep or the ceiling.

from: The table counts.
It lists houses damaged and dollars claimed.
It shows how bad each case was.
It has no geography, so one hard-hit street does not show.
to: The table counts.
Houses damaged, dollars claimed, days out of the home — it distinguishes severity, and it has no geography at all, so you cannot see that one street took most of it.

expand.kernel: A budget built on the average will not reach those twenty.
expand.expanded: A budget drawn from the average will not reach the twenty, and a budget drawn from the photograph will not reach the rest.

expand.kernel: So ask which document the decision comes from.
expand.expanded: So the question for the meeting is which document the decision is being made from.

from: A population pyramid is two bar charts back to back.
Men are on one side and women on the other.
Age rises from the bottom.
The shape tells you a lot.
to: A population pyramid is two bar charts laid back to back, men on one side and women on the other, with age rising from the bottom.
The shape alone tells you most of what a country is about to face.

from: Notches are history.
A pinch in one age band marks a war or a famine.
That band also had fewer children.
So the pinch shows up again higher up.
to: Notches are history.
A pinch in one age band marks a war, a famine, or a policy, and because that band also had fewer children, the pinch reappears twenty-five years higher up.

items.title: The Chart in the Doctor's Office

from: Crossing lines gets attention.
A child who moves from the fiftieth to the tenth has not become short.
Something has changed.
Two dots were compared, not just read.
to: Crossing lines is what gets attention.
A child who moves from the fiftieth to the tenth over two years has not become short; something has changed, and the chart found it because two dots were compared and not just read.

from: A growth chart is a sheet of curved lines.
A child's height is a dot among them.
Parents read the dot.
Doctors read which line it follows.
to: A growth chart is a sheet of curved lines, and a child's height is a dot somewhere among them.
Parents read the dot.
Doctors read which line it is following.

from: The fast wave comes first.
P waves move through rock at about six kilometers a second.
S waves follow at about half that.
The gap between them gives the distance.
to: The fast wave comes first.
P waves travel through rock at about six kilometers a second; S waves follow at roughly half that, and the gap between them on the trace is the only thing needed to find the distance.

from: Three stations give a point.
Three circles cross in one place.
That crossing is the epicenter.
One instrument is useless and several are precise.
to: Three stations give a point.
Three circles cross in one place, and that intersection is the epicenter, which is why a seismic network is useless with one instrument and precise with several.

items.title: Should the City Build a Bike Lane?

from: The plan would turn one of four traffic lanes into a protected bike lane.
The council packet runs eleven pages.
Four claims carry evidence.
Three do not.
to: The proposal would take one of four traffic lanes on Market Street and make it a protected bike lane.
The council packet runs eleven pages.
Four of its claims carry evidence and three do not.

from: The supported ones are easy to check.
The city counted 1,340 cyclists a day in September.
The fire department wrote that a protected lane still fits an engine.
to: The supported ones are easy to check.
The city counted 1,340 cyclists a day on Market Street in September, and the fire department's own letter says a protected lane does not narrow the path for an engine.

expand.kernel: Taking a lane away and expecting no change could be tested.
expand.expanded: Taking a lane away and expecting no change in traffic is a claim that could be tested, cheaply, by measuring Oak Street before and after.

expand.kernel: The property values are a hope.
expand.expanded: The property values are a hope with a sentence around it.

expand.kernel: An argument can be worth supporting and badly made.
expand.expanded: An argument can be worth supporting and badly made at the same time.

items.title: The Claim That Sharks Do Not Get Cancer

from: The first step is false.
A registry has recorded dozens of tumors in sharks.
Some were cancers of the cartilage itself.
They were on record before the book.
to: The first step is false.
The Registry of Tumors in Lower Animals has documented dozens of tumors in sharks, including cancers of the cartilage itself, which were on record before the book was written.

from: The third step does not follow either.
A substance in an animal is not a drug you can swallow.
Cartilage is mostly protein.
Protein is digested.
to: The third step does not follow even if the first two did.
A substance in an animal's body is not a drug you can swallow; cartilage is mostly protein, and protein is digested rather than delivered.

from: The safety claim is weaker than it sounds.
City water is tested more often than bottled water.
That is true.
It does not make every tap safe.
Flint had tested water and a lead problem.
to: The safety claim is weaker than the flyer suggests.
Municipal water in the United States is tested more often than bottled water is, which is true, and that does not make every tap safe — Flint had tested water and a lead problem.

from: The cost claim is solid.
A gallon from the tap costs a fraction of a cent.
The same gallon in bottles costs a few dollars.
Anyone can check that on a bill.
to: The cost claim is solid.
A gallon from the tap costs a fraction of a cent in most American cities, and the same gallon in bottles runs a few dollars, which is a comparison anyone can check on a bill.

items.title: The Advertisement for the Memory Pill

from: It opens with a doctor.
The photograph shows a person in a white coat.
The name has letters after it.
Nothing says what the letters mean.
to: It opens with a doctor.
The photograph is of a person in a white coat, the name has letters after it, and nothing says what the letters are or whether the person studied memory.

from: A full-page advertisement promises better memory in thirty days.
It reads like an argument.
It is built from things that are not evidence.
to: A full-page advertisement promises better memory in thirty days.
It reads like an argument and is built out of things that are not evidence.

from: Two sides filed statements with the county about an eighty-year-old dam.
Both argue honestly.
Both argue from different things they can prove.
to: Two sides filed written statements with the county about an eighty-year-old dam, and both are arguing honestly from different things they can prove.

from: They also say the dam is unsafe.
That claim is borrowed.
It rests on an inspection of a different dam from the same decade.
That is a reason to inspect, not a finding.
to: They also claim the dam is unsafe, and that one is borrowed.
It rests on a state inspection of a different dam built the same decade, which is a reason to inspect this one and not a finding about it.

expand.kernel: So the strongest claim on each side is specific and local.
expand.expanded: So the strongest claim on each side is specific and local, and the weakest on each side is general and borrowed.

from: The memoir is written forward.
Shackleton tells it as he lived it.
The reader does not know whether the boat journey will work.
At the time he did not know either.
to: The memoir is written forward.
Shackleton tells it as he lived it, so the reader does not know whether the boat journey will work, because at the time he did not either.

from: They disagree about people.
Shackleton is generous to nearly everyone aboard.
The crew's diaries name the men who would not work.
The biography uses them.
to: They disagree about people.
Shackleton's book is generous to nearly everyone aboard; the crew's own diaries name the men who would not work, and the biography uses them.

expand.kernel: It carries what it felt like to be cold for eighteen months.
expand.expanded: It carries what it felt like to be cold for eighteen months, and no amount of research reproduces that.

items.title: Two Accounts of the Triangle Fire

from: The newspaper counts and locates.
It gives the floor and the time of the alarm.
It gives the number of bodies on the sidewalk.
It says the ladders reached six floors short.
to: The newspaper counts and locates.
It gives the floor, the time the alarm came in, the number of bodies on the sidewalk, and the height the ladders reached, which was six floors short.

from: The pamphlet uses different nouns.
It calls the deaths a crime.
It names the two owners.
It prints that the ninth floor door opened inward and was locked.
to: The pamphlet uses different nouns.
It calls the deaths a crime, names the two owners, and prints the fact that the ninth floor door opened inward and was locked.

expand.kernel: They differ on whether it was a fact about the building or something somebody did.
expand.expanded: What differs is whether the door is something that was true of the building or something somebody did, and that is a choice about nouns before it is a choice about facts.

expand.kernel: The pamphlet ends with a demand for factory inspection laws.
expand.expanded: The pamphlet ends with a demand for factory inspection laws, which is what the fire eventually produced.

from: He gives the sequence too.
First the cloud.
Then ash and pumice falling.
Then the dark.
Then something came down the mountain fast and killed his uncle.
to: He gives the sequence too.
First the cloud, then ash and pumice falling, then the dark, then something that came down the mountain fast and killed his uncle on the shore.

from: The paper gives the numbers.
The column reached about thirty-three kilometers.
The fall deposit is sorted by size.
The fast thing is named a pyroclastic flow.
to: The paper gives the numbers.
The column reached about thirty-three kilometers, the fall deposit is graded by size, and the fast thing that came down is named a pyroclastic flow and timed by layer.

expand.kernel: This eruption style is called Plinian, after a boy who got the shape right.
expand.expanded: This eruption style is called Plinian, after a boy who got the shape right and the distances wrong.

items.title: Two Accounts of the Challenger Decision

from: The report is organized by cause.
It shows that a rubber O-ring failed in the cold.
It documents the temperature.
It rebuilds the decision meeting from transcripts.
to: The commission report is organized by cause.
It establishes that a rubber O-ring failed in the cold, documents the temperature, and reconstructs the decision meeting from transcripts and testimony.

from: The engineer's account is organized by the night before.
He writes what he said.
He writes who stopped listening.
His management asked him to take off his engineering hat.
to: The engineer's account is organized by the night before.
He writes what he said, who stopped listening, and the moment his own management asked him to take off his engineering hat.

items.title: Two Accounts of the Jamestown Winter

from: The winter of 1609 killed about three-quarters of the people at Jamestown.
Two men who were there wrote about it.
They were enemies.
to: The winter of 1609 killed about three-quarters of the people at Jamestown.
Two men who were there wrote about it, and they were enemies.

from: John Smith had been forced out before the winter began.
His account blames the men who replaced him.
He was not there for the season he describes.
to: John Smith had been forced out of the colony before the winter began.
His account blames the men who replaced him, and he was not present for the season he describes.

items.stem: Smith does not dwell on leaving.

from: The first stage is fast.
Hagfish, sharks and amphipods strip the soft tissue.
A body can lose most of its flesh within months.
Scavengers arrive from kilometers away.
to: The first stage is fast.
Hagfish, sleeper sharks and amphipods strip the soft tissue, and a carcass can lose most of its flesh within months, with scavengers arriving from kilometers away.

from: Then the bones become the habitat.
A whale skeleton is about sixty percent fat by weight.
The bones themselves are full of it.
That fat is the slow fuel.
to: Then the bones become the habitat.
A whale skeleton is about sixty percent lipid by weight, which is to say the bones themselves are full of fat, and that fat is the slow fuel.

items.title: Mapping the Source of the Nile

from: The question was never really geographic.
It was a competition.
The prize was the name attached to the answer.
That is why the 1850s expeditions are remembered as a quarrel.
to: The question was never really geographic.
It was a competition, and the prize was the name attached to the answer, which is why the expeditions of the 1850s are remembered as a quarrel.

from: Burton was right about the proof.
Speke had seen one lake.
He had not followed the river out of it.
That is the only way to show a lake feeds a river.
to: Burton was right about the proof.
Speke had seen one lake and had not followed the river out of it, which is the only way to show that a lake feeds a particular river.

expand.kernel: What changed was which library held a paper saying so.
expand.expanded: What changed in 1858 was not where the Nile came from but which library held a paper saying so.

items.title: How Elephants Talk Through the Ground

from: The calls are infrasound, below about twenty hertz.
Low sounds carry further than high ones.
They lose less energy to the air.
That is why distant thunder is a rumble.
to: The calls are infrasound, below about twenty hertz.
Low frequencies carry further than high ones because they lose less energy to the air, which is why distant thunder is a rumble and never a crack.

from: The sound also travels in the ground.
A rumble sets up a wave in the soil.
That wave outruns the one in the air.
It arrives first and carries further.
to: The sound also travels in the ground.
A rumble sets up a surface wave in the soil, and that wave outruns the airborne one, arriving first and carrying further still.

from: The cause was a reform.
Flush toilets had spread through London over twenty years.
Every one of them emptied into a drain.
The drains ran into the river.
to: The cause was a reform.
Flush toilets had spread through London in the previous twenty years, and every one of them emptied into a cesspool or a drain that ran, eventually, into the river.

from: People blamed the smell itself.
Miasma theory said disease rose from foul air.
That was wrong about the cause.
It happened to recommend the right action.
to: The accepted explanation was the smell itself.
Miasma theory held that disease rose from foul air, which was wrong about the mechanism and happened to recommend the right action.

from: The material came from a squirrel burrow thirty-eight meters down.
It was found in a riverbank.
It was packed with fruits an animal had stored and never came back for.
to: The material came from a squirrel burrow thirty-eight meters down, found in a riverbank, packed with fruits and seeds an animal had stored and never returned to.

from: The seeds themselves would not sprout.
The team used tissue from inside immature fruit instead.
They grew it on in culture.
That route is slower and it worked.
to: The seeds themselves would not germinate.
The team worked instead from placental tissue inside immature fruit, grown on in culture, which is a slower route and the one that worked.
